512.title: Six of Shawwal
512.hook: six fasts after Ramadan are like fasting the year (Muslim)
512.howItsDone: Many Muslims fast six voluntary days in Shawwal, the month after Ramadan, starting after the day of Eid; some fast them consecutively and others spread them through the month.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the takbirat of Eid, and your line was allahu akbar on the way. Did you say it, even under your breath, on your way somewhere? Day five hundred twelve.

The morning after Eid, the house looks like a party happened. Plates in the sink, sweets nobody can face, new clothes hung back up. For thirty days the whole rhythm of life was different: the pre-dawn meal, the long afternoon, the date at sunset, the night prayer. And now, suddenly, lunch is back. Some people feel relief. Plenty feel a strange little grief, as if a guest left without saying goodbye. The month after Ramadan is called Shawwal, and there's a quiet custom tucked into it that many Muslims keep: not one more month of fasting, just six more days.

The custom rests on one hadith. In Sahih Muslim, the companion Abu Ayyub al-Ansari reports that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said that whoever fasts Ramadan and then follows it with six days of Shawwal, it is as if they had fasted for the whole span of time. Another report, from the companion Thawban, gives the arithmetic behind it. A good deed is counted ten times over, a principle the Qur'an itself states. So thirty days of Ramadan count as three hundred, and six more count as sixty. Three hundred and sixty: roughly a year. A year's fast, folded into five weeks. There are a few practical things people learn quickly. You don't fast on the day of Eid itself; the Prophet forbade fasting on the two Eids. After that, the six can be kept back to back, right after Eid, or spread through the month, a Monday here, a Thursday there. Scholars have discussed both, and many say either is fine. And people who missed days of Ramadan, through illness, travel, or for women, their monthly period, often ask which comes first, making up the missed days or the six. Here the schools give different answers, and many people simply ask a scholar they trust. Not everyone in early Islam was enthusiastic, either. Imam Malik, the great scholar of Medina, is reported to have disliked making it a fixed custom, worried people might start treating it as part of Ramadan. Most of the other major schools recommend it. What the six do, for those who keep them, is keep the door from slamming shut. Ramadan ends, but the habit doesn't vanish overnight. A small part of it stays in the week.
screen: `ONE HADITH, IN SAHIH MUSLIM.` · `THIRTY TIMES TEN, PLUS SIX TIMES TEN.` · `NOT ON EID; TOGETHER OR SPREAD OUT.` · `KEEP THE DOOR FROM SLAMMING SHUT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one fast. Sit, and let the breath settle. Picture next week. Find one day that's calm enough, no big dinner, no hard workout. If you're able, and it's safe for your health, decide to fast it, from dawn to sunset. If fasting isn't possible for you, choose one thing to give up for that day instead, and pick what you'll do with the time it frees. Write the day down somewhere you'll see it. If you pray, you can make your intention quietly now. The bell holds the time.
Six of Shawwal. The six voluntary fasts many Muslims keep in the month after Ramadan, which the hadith counts, with Ramadan, as a whole year. Today's word.
Your line: six more. Today, keep one small Ramadan habit going, the early prayer, the extra page, the shared plate, just for one more day. Day five hundred twelve.

513.title: The ten days
513.hook: no days are dearer to Allah for good deeds than the first ten of Dhul Hijjah (Bukhari)
513.howItsDone: In the first ten days of Dhul Hijjah many Muslims increase prayer, charity, remembrance and takbir; many fast the day of 'Arafah, and some fast the first nine days.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Six of Shawwal, and your line was six more. Which small Ramadan habit did you keep going for one more day? Day five hundred thirteen.

Ask most people which days of the Islamic year are the holiest and they'll say Ramadan, and they'd be right that its nights carry Laylat al-Qadr. But there's a hadith that surprises people the first time they hear it. It names a different stretch of days, about two months after Ramadan ends, at the start of the last month of the year, the month of pilgrimage. While millions of pilgrims are heading for Mecca, everyone else, at home, is also in a season. Today: the ten days.

In Sahih al-Bukhari, Ibn 'Abbas reports that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said there are no days in which good deeds are more beloved to God than these, meaning the first ten days of Dhul Hijjah. The companions were startled. Not even striving in the path of God? Not even that, he said, except a man who goes out with his life and his wealth and comes back with nothing. It's a striking answer. An ordinary good deed, done in these ten days, is set beside the hardest sacrifice there is. Many commentators also connect the days to the Qur'an. Surah Al-Fajr opens with an oath, by the dawn, and ten nights, and a long line of commentators understood those ten nights as these. And Surah Al-Hajj speaks of remembering God's name on appointed days, which Ibn 'Abbas is reported to have explained as the ten. What do people actually do? They do more of what they already do. Extra prayer, charity, reading, kindness. Some fast the first nine days. Many fast at least the ninth, the day of 'Arafah, when the pilgrims stand on the plain; a hadith in Sahih Muslim hopes that fast wipes away the faults of the year before and the year after. Some companions, Bukhari notes, used to walk through the markets in these days saying the takbir aloud, and people around them took it up. And a hadith in Muslim says that someone planning to offer a sacrifice for Eid shouldn't cut their hair or nails from the start of the month, a small mark in the body that the season has begun. The point isn't a new set of rules. It's a window: the same deeds, in a season when they weigh more.
screen: `NO DAYS DEARER FOR GOOD DEEDS.` · `BY THE DAWN, AND TEN NIGHTS.` · `THE FAST OF 'ARAFAH.` · `THE SAME DEEDS, A HEAVIER SEASON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one extra good, each day. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of ten days, starting today. Choose one small good you could add to each of them. Not a heroic one. A text to someone who's lonely. A coin in a box. Ten minutes of reading. Picking up litter on the walk home. Pick something you can actually do ten times. Picture yourself doing it on day seven, when you're tired. If it still fits, keep it. If you pray, you can make your intention now. The bell holds the time.
The ten days. The first ten of Dhul Hijjah, the month of pilgrimage, when, in the hadith, good deeds are dearer to God than on any other days. Today's word.
Your line: the best ten days. Today, do the first of your ten small goods, and mark it somewhere so day two remembers. Day five hundred thirteen.

514.title: Eid al-Adha: days of tashriq
514.hook: takbir after prayers for the days after Eid
514.howItsDone: On Eid al-Adha Muslims who are able offer an animal sacrifice and share the meat with family, neighbors and people in need; many say the takbir after the daily prayers through the days of tashriq, the eleventh to thirteenth of Dhul Hijjah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ten days, and your line was the best ten days. Did you mark your first small good somewhere, so the next day could find it? Day five hundred fourteen.

In a lot of Muslim homes, the morning of Eid al-Adha has a particular sound. Not just greetings and children, but bags. Plastic bags of meat being divided on the kitchen counter, knotted, labeled, carried next door, driven across town, dropped at a cousin's, handed to the man who sweeps the street. Phones buzzing with addresses. Someone always asking whether the neighbors on the third floor got theirs. It's the feast of the sacrifice, and it doesn't end in one day. Today: Eid al-Adha, and the days that follow it.
screen: `A FEAST THAT DOESN'T END IN A DAY.`

segments.voice: Eid al-Adha falls on the tenth of Dhul Hijjah, the day after the pilgrims stand at 'Arafah. Adha comes from the word for the sacrifice offered in the forenoon. It remembers Ibrahim, who in Surah As-Saffat saw in a dream that he was to sacrifice his son, and both of them submitted, and God ransomed the son with a tremendous sacrifice. Muslims who are able offer an animal, a sheep, a goat, a share in a cow or camel, and the Qur'an tells them in Surah Al-Hajj to eat of it and to feed the one who is content and the one who asks. Many divide it in thirds: for the household, for friends and neighbors, and for those in need, a custom scholars recommend rather than require. The same surah adds a line people quote every year: neither the flesh nor the blood reaches God; what reaches Him is your devotion, your taqwa. Then come three more days, the eleventh, twelfth and thirteenth, called the days of tashriq. The name is usually explained from drying strips of meat in the sun. A hadith in Sahih Muslim describes them in a phrase that became today's line: they are days of eating and drinking, and of remembering God. Fasting is not allowed on them. And the remembrance has a shape. Surah Al-Baqarah says to remember God through the numbered days, and many Muslims say the takbir after each of the five daily prayers, from the dawn of 'Arafah until the afternoon of the thirteenth: God is greatest, God is greatest, there is no god but God. The schools differ a little on the exact start and end. So a feast, a share for the neighbor, and a refrain after every prayer, four days running.
screen: `THE TENTH: IBRAHIM'S RANSOM.` · `EAT, AND FEED THE ONE WHO ASKS.` · `NOT THE FLESH: THE DEVOTION.` · `THREE DAYS OF TASHRIQ.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: share food with a neighbor. Sit, and let the breath settle. Picture the people who live closest to you. The door across the hall, the house over the fence, the colleague at the next desk. Pick one, maybe someone you've never really spoken to. Decide what you could bring them this week. It needn't be meat or anything grand. A plate of something you cooked, a box of fruit, tea you like. Picture handing it over. If you pray, you can say God is greatest, quietly, as you imagine it. The bell holds the time.
Eid al-Adha. The feast of the sacrifice on the tenth of Dhul Hijjah, remembering Ibrahim's ransom, followed by the three days of tashriq. Today's word.
Your line: eat, drink, remember. Today, at one meal, before you eat, stop for one breath and remember where it came from. Day five hundred fourteen.

515.title: A moving calendar
515.hook: a lunar year is about eleven days shorter, so Ramadan visits every season over thirty-three years
515.tomorrow: Who feeds me and heals me
515.howItsDone: Muslims date Ramadan, Hajj and the other holy days by the lunar Hijri calendar, beginning months by sighting or calculating the new crescent, so the festivals move about eleven days earlier each solar year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Eid al-Adha and the days of tashriq, and your line was eat, drink, remember. Which meal did you stop before, for one breath? Day five hundred fifteen, the last day of the holy days.

Ask a Muslim in their fifties about Ramadan as a child, and you may hear about a different season. Long summer days, the fast running past eight in the evening, playing outside in the heat with a dry mouth. Ask someone in their thirties and they might remember short winter fasts, breaking it at five, homework by lamplight. Same month, same rules, a completely different experience. That's not a change in the religion. It's the calendar, doing exactly what it was built to do.

The Hijri calendar follows the moon. Each month begins when the new crescent, the hilal, is seen or reckoned. Twelve lunar months add up to about three hundred fifty-four days, roughly eleven days shorter than the solar year. So every year, Ramadan arrives about eleven days earlier by the solar calendar. Over roughly thirty-three years, it slides backward through every season, and comes round again. The Qur'an names this rhythm. In Surah Al-Baqarah people ask about the new moons, and the answer is that they are markers of time for people and for the pilgrimage. Surah At-Tawbah says the number of months with God is twelve. And the same surah criticizes the practice called nasi', postponing a month; many historians understand that as an older Arabian habit of adjusting the calendar so the months stayed put. The Qur'anic calendar lets them move. Here's what that does. Nobody's Ramadan is always the hard one, or always the easy one. Over a lifetime, someone in the far north gets long summer fasts and short winter ones; someone in the southern hemisphere has them the other way round. Hajj, too, travels through the seasons. And the moon is something anyone can see, from a roof or a field, without a printed calendar. Looking back over these two weeks, the holy days have moved with it: the Hijri new year, 'Ashura's two memories, Mawlid, the night journey, Sha'ban's getting ready, Ramadan's book and seclusion and khatm, the takbir of Eid, six more, the ten days, and the feast of the sacrifice. Every one of them drifts through the seasons, together. Tomorrow we go back to the book, to the middle of the Qur'an.
screen: `TWELVE MONTHS BY THE MOON.` · `ELEVEN DAYS EARLIER EACH YEAR.` · `EVERY SEASON IN THIRTY-THREE YEARS.` · `THE HOLY DAYS MOVE TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find Ramadan on the year. Sit, and let the breath settle. Look out the window, or picture it. What season is it where you are? Now think about when Ramadan falls in the current year, or look it up afterward. Is it a season of long days or short ones, heat or cold, school or holidays? Then let your mind run thirty-three years forward. The same month will have visited every one of those seasons by then. Who will you be? If you pray, you can hold that thought as a quiet hope. The bell holds the time.

516.title: Who feeds me and heals me
516.word: Who feeds me and heals me
516.hook: Ibrahim describes his Lord: who created me, guides me, feeds me, and heals me when I'm ill (26:78–80)
516.carry: he feeds me; he heals me
516.howItsDone: Many Muslims say bismillah before eating and alhamdulillah after, and pray for the sick with words from the Prophet's practice that name God as the Healer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a moving calendar, and your line was ramadan visits every season. Did you find the moon, and what shape was it in? Day five hundred sixteen, and a new block begins.

We're back in the book, and in its middle. This block runs from Surah Ash-Shu'ara, the Poets, the twenty-sixth, through the surahs that follow it. Ash-Shu'ara is long and full of prophets: Musa, Ibrahim, Nuh, Hud, Salih, Lut, Shu'ayb. After each story comes the same refrain, that in this is a sign, and that your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful. Today's verses come from Ibrahim's story. He asks his father and his people what they worship. They say idols, and that their fathers did the same. And Ibrahim answers by describing, very simply, the One he worships.
screen: `BLOCK C: THE MIDDLE OF THE BOOK.`
`A SURAH OF PROPHETS AND A REFRAIN.`

segments.voice: Ibrahim's answer is made of verbs, and in Arabic nearly every one ends in the sound for me: created me, guides me, feeds me, heals me. Pickthall: "Who created me, and He doth guide me, And Who feedeth me and watereth me. And when I sicken, then He healeth me." Then he goes on: who causes me to die and then gives me life, and who, he hopes, will forgive his faults on the Day of Judgment. Look at what he picks. Not the stars or the mountains. The things a person lives through every day. Being made. Being shown the way. Breakfast. A glass of water. A fever that breaks. It's a whole theology at the level of the kitchen table. Then there's a small detail in the grammar. Every line says He did it: He created, He guides, He feeds, He gives drink. Until the illness. There Ibrahim doesn't say, when He makes me sick. He says, when I sicken. Many commentators read that as adab, courtesy: he speaks of God in connection with the good, and takes the hard thing onto himself. Not as a theory of where illness comes from, but as a way of speaking. And the healing goes straight back to God. The same shape runs through how many Muslims pray for the sick: the illness named plainly, the healing asked of God. A hadith in Bukhari records the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, visiting the sick, asking God, the Healer, to heal, with a healing that leaves no illness behind. The words in Ibrahim's mouth are short. But they cover a life: made, guided, fed, given drink, healed, and in the end, he hopes, forgiven.
screen: `MADE, GUIDED, FED, GIVEN DRINK.` · `A THEOLOGY OF THE KITCHEN TABLE.` · `WHEN I SICKEN: A COURTESY.` · `THEN HE HEALS ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank Him at your next meal. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think about the last thing you ate. Where did it come from? The field, the hands that picked it, the truck, the shop, whoever cooked it. Then the last glass of water. Then think of the last time you were ill and got better. Go through Ibrahim's list slowly: made, guided, fed, given drink, healed. Stay with whichever one lands. If you pray, you can say thank you for it now, and again before you next eat. The bell holds the time.
Who feeds me and heals me. Ibrahim's description of his Lord in Ash-Shu'ara: the One who made him, guides him, feeds him, gives him drink, and heals him when he falls ill. Today's word.

517.title: A sound heart
517.hook: the Day when wealth and sons won't help, only one who comes with a sound heart (26:88–89)
517.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite Ibrahim's prayer from Ash-Shu'ara and ask God for a sound heart, and some make a habit of forgiving others before sleeping.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ibrahim's words, and your line was he feeds me; he heals me. Whose hands did you name before your first bite? Day five hundred seventeen.

Airports have a rule about what you can carry on. A small bag, a weight limit, and a whole list of things that have to be left behind at the gate. People stand at the security tray deciding, fast, what really matters. Ibrahim's prayer in Ash-Shu'ara keeps going after yesterday's verses, and it ends at a kind of gate. A day when almost everything people spend their lives collecting has to be left on the other side. There's only one thing he says gets through.

Ibrahim asks for wisdom, for good company, for an honest name among those who come later, for forgiveness for his father. Then he asks not to be disgraced on the day people are raised, and describes that day. Pickthall: "The day when wealth and sons avail not (any man) Save him who bringeth unto Allah a whole heart." Pickthall says a whole heart. The Arabic is qalb salim. Qalb is heart, and its root carries the sense of turning over, which early scholars noticed, since hearts turn. Salim comes from the root s-l-m, the same root as salam, peace, and islam, surrender. It means sound, safe, intact, unbroken. So what makes a heart salim? Commentators gave several answers, and they stack. Free of associating anything with God. Free of doubt. And many added: free of malice, envy and grudges toward other people. The Qur'an uses the same phrase once more, in As-Saffat, of Ibrahim himself: he came to his Lord with a sound heart. So he's asking for what he already had, which may be the point; nobody counts their heart finished. There's a hadith in both Bukhari and Muslim that sits right beside this verse. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said that in the body there is a lump of flesh; when it is sound, the whole body is sound, and when it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt, and it is the heart. Wealth and children are good things in the Qur'an. They just don't come through the gate. What comes through is a heart, and whether it arrives in one piece.
screen: `WEALTH AND SONS AVAIL NOT.` · `QALB: THE HEART THAT TURNS.` · `SALIM: SOUND, SAFE, INTACT.` · `FREE OF SHIRK, DOUBT AND GRUDGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: clear one grudge. Sit, and let the breath settle. Let a face come to mind, someone you're still a little sore with. Don't pick the worst wound you have; pick a small one, something you could actually set down. Notice where you carry it, in your jaw, your shoulders, your stomach. Breathe into that place. You don't have to excuse what happened. Just loosen your grip on it for this minute. If you pray, you can ask for a sound heart, and for good for that person. The bell holds the time.
Qalb salim. A sound heart, whole and safe, free of shirk, doubt and grudge: the one thing Ibrahim says avails on the Day. Today's word.

fork.setup: you're standing at the gate on the Day Ibrahim describes. you can bring one thing through. what is it?
options: your wealth.
your children's success.
a sound heart.
fork.reveal: 26:88–89: wealth and sons avail not, save him who brings to God a whole, sound heart.

original.note: Arabic: qalb salim, a sound heart; salim is from s-l-m, the root of salam and islam.

trapdoor: what you thought: a healthy heart, maybe a good person.
what it means: a heart that arrives whole, free of shirk and doubt, and for many commentators free of grudges too.
what a scholar hears: the phrase appears twice, at 26:89 and at 37:84 of Ibrahim himself; commentators listed shirk, doubt, malice and envy as what a salim heart is free of.

518.title: Lower your wing
518.hook: lower your wing to the believers who follow you (26:215)
518.howItsDone: Muslims read 26:215 alongside the Prophet's example of humility with his companions, and many quote the parallel verse in Al-Isra about lowering the wing of humility to one's parents.

segments.voice: Yesterday, qalb salim, and your line was bring a sound heart. Did you do the small, quiet kindness for the person you were sore with? Day five hundred eighteen, the end of the week.

Watch a hen when the sky darkens. She doesn't make a speech. She crouches, spreads her wings low, and the chicks run under. Watch a big bird coming in to land, and it does something similar: it lowers its wings, slows down, and comes close to the ground. A raised wing is for flying, for display, for looking big. A lowered wing is for landing, and for covering someone. Near the end of Ash-Shu'ara, after all the prophets' stories, the surah turns to the Prophet himself, and gives him that picture.

The verses come in a row. First: warn your nearest kin. Many reports say that after this the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ climbed the hill of Safa in Mecca and called the clans of Quraysh by name. Then, right after the warning, comes tenderness. Pickthall: "And lower thy wing (in kindness) unto those believers who follow thee." Pickthall adds in kindness in brackets, because the Arabic picture, khafd al-janah, lowering the wing, already means it: gentleness, humility, coming down to someone's level. Notice who it's addressed to. The leader. The one everybody follows. It's not, follow humbly. It's, lead humbly. The Qur'an uses the same image for children and parents in Al-Isra: lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy. There the young lower the wing to the old. Here the one in charge lowers it to those who look up to him. Either way, the person with the power to fly over others is told to come down and cover them. And the sira, the story of his life, is full of small examples: mending his own sandal, sitting with the poor, answering an old woman who stopped him in the street. This week was a slow landing after the holy days. Six more fasts. The best ten days. Eat, drink, remember. A calendar that moves through every season. Then back to the book: he feeds me, he heals me; bring a sound heart. And today, lower the wing.
screen: `FIRST: WARN YOUR NEAREST KIN.` · `KHAFD AL-JANAH: LOWER THE WING.` · `NOT FOLLOW HUMBLY: LEAD HUMBLY.` · `PARENTS, AND THOSE WHO FOLLOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: lower your wing to someone who looks up to you. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of someone who sees you as a little ahead of them. A younger sibling, a new colleague, a student, your own child, someone you mentor without calling it that. How do you usually speak to them? Quickly? From above? Picture one ordinary moment with them, and replay it with your wing lowered: sitting at their height, listening first, asking instead of telling. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Lower your wing. The Qur'an's picture of gentleness from above: a leader coming down, like a bird landing, to cover those who follow. Today's word.
Your line: lower the wing. Today, with the person you just pictured, listen all the way to the end of what they're saying before you answer. Day five hundred eighteen.

fork.setup: you're the one everybody follows. the Qur'an has just told you to warn your nearest kin. what comes next?
options: raise your voice so they take you seriously.
lower your wing to those who follow you.
keep your distance to keep respect.
fork.reveal: 26:215 comes straight after the warning: lower thy wing unto those believers who follow thee.

original.note: Arabic: 'and lower your wing'; janah is wing, khafd is lowering.

trapdoor: what you thought: an odd bird metaphor.
what it means: gentleness from the one with power, coming down to cover those who follow, the way a bird lands or a hen shelters chicks.
what a scholar hears: khafd al-janah appears at 26:215, 15:88 and, for parents, at 17:24; 26:214's warning to kin is linked in the sira to the call from Safa.
